payload.question: The IFSCA FME framework recognises which categories of Fund Management Entities?

options.text: Authorised FME, Registered FME (Non-Retail) and Registered FME (Retail)

options.text: Launch Venture Capital Schemes and restricted schemes, and offer Portfolio Management Services
Launch Venture Capital Schemes for accredited/threshold investors, and manage a Family Investment Fund for a Single Family
Launch retail schemes and exchange traded funds, and manage a Family Investment Fund for a Single Family
Manage a Family Investment Fund for several unrelated families, and act as investment manager for private placements

activities.title: 2022 vs 2025 — The VC Investor Count Trap

payload.provision_text: Venture Capital schemes shall have less than fifty (50) investors.
payload.question: Is this the 2022 position or the current 2025 position?

answer.explanation: 2022 position — maximum 49 investors ("less than fifty"). The 2025 regulations say "shall not have more than fifty (50)" — maximum 50. A scheme with exactly 50 investors: non-compliant under 2022, compliant under 2025.

activities.title: VC Minimum Investment — Above or At Least?

payload.question: Under the current 2025 regulations, a non-accredited investor may invest in a Venture Capital scheme by investing:

options.text: Above USD 250,000 — strictly more than the threshold, as under the 2022 regulations
At least USD 150,000
Any amount, if the scheme has fewer than 50 investors
At least USD 250,000 — exactly USD 250,000 qualifies

answer.explanation: 2025 requires "at least USD 250,000", so exactly USD 250,000 qualifies; 2022's "above USD 250,000" excluded it. Employees/directors/designated partners: minimum USD 60,000. USD 150,000 is the lower application size that pushes a scheme into the restricted route.

payload.scenario:
Meridian Capital IFSC Pvt. Ltd., a Registered FME (Non-Retail) in GIFT City, filed a placement memorandum for a close-ended restricted scheme (Category II AIF). IFSCA communicated that the PPM was taken on record on 15 February 2025.

By early 2026, the scheme had raised only USD 1.8 Million against the minimum corpus requirement. On 25 February 2026, the FME filed an application with IFSCA to extend the PPM validity by six months, enclosing a fee equal to 50% of the fresh scheme filing fee.

The compliance officer signed off, noting: "One-time 6-month extension available under Regulation 31 — we're covered."
payload.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the extension is valid, since a one-time six-month extension at a 50% fee remains available
Only the fee is wrong — it should have been 25% of the fresh-scheme filing fee for a first extension
The application is fatally late — it had to be filed while the PPM was still valid — and the fee and the CO's position are outdated
The scheme should simply have declared its first close at the USD 1.8 Million it had already raised

payload.provision_text: An individual with post-qualification experience of at least 2 (two) years in an eligible institution in IFSC, India or any foreign jurisdiction and who holds valid certification(s), as specified by the Authority, shall be considered eligible for the KMP referred under sub-regulation (2).
payload.question: Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

The 2026 Amendment substituted clause (b) of the KMP experience requirement and introduced graded routes: 5 years' experience in an "eligible institution" (a newly defined term), reduced to 3 years where the KMP holds a professional qualification, and a 2-year post-qualification route where the individual holds Authority-specified certifications. The pre-amendment text simply required 5 years in related securities-market activities.

cards.title: Three doors into GIFT City fund management
cards.law: The framework recognises Authorised FMEs, Registered FMEs (Non-Retail) and Registered FMEs (Retail).
cards.means: An ascending ladder of trust. Authorised: VC schemes and single-family funds. Non-Retail adds restricted schemes, PMS and private REIT/InvIT management. Retail sits on top: retail schemes, ETFs, public REIT/InvIT offers — plus everything below.
cards.trip: Each tier inherits ALL activities of the tiers beneath it. A Retail FME never needs a second registration to run a VC scheme.
cards.hook: Think 3 doors, each opening every door before it.

cards.title: The net worth ladder
cards.law: Minimum net worth: USD 75,000 (Authorised), USD 500,000 (Non-Retail), USD 1,000,000 (Retail) — at all times.
cards.means: The price of each door. And it is a continuous obligation — dipping below the line mid-year is a breach even if you were compliant at registration.
cards.trip: Branches hold net worth at the PARENT level — but the parent must ensure the branch has operating funds. And FME net worth is separate from and additional to net worth needed for any other regulated activity.
cards.hook: 75K → 500K → 1M: roughly ×7, then ×2.

cards.title: Getting in, switching, getting out
cards.law: Deficient applications get 30 days to cure. Category change needs prior Authority approval. Surrender is effective only on acceptance.
cards.means: IFSCA controls all three gates. You cannot drift between categories by conduct, and you remain a regulated (and liable) entity until the Authority formally accepts your exit.
cards.trip: Meeting the higher net worth does NOT auto-upgrade you — Reg. 13(2) requires prior approval for any category change.
cards.link: Prior-approval logic returns for retail fiduciaries (Module 5) and business expansion (Module 11).

cards.title: Stay in your lane
cards.law: An FME shall not undertake business activities other than those specified, without prior approval of the Authority.
cards.means: The activity perimeter is closed by default. Even a branch acting on its home regulator’s approval for an outside-IFSC activity must inform IFSCA within 15 days.
cards.trip: Opening a marketing or client-service office in another jurisdiction needs PRIOR intimation — not post-facto.

cards.title: Two people every FME must have
cards.law: Every FME appoints a Principal Officer — responsible overall for fund management, risk management and compliance — and an additional KMP designated as Compliance Officer.
cards.means: The PO is the apex accountable human; the CO is the professional conscience. Between them, everything the FME does has a name attached to it.
cards.trip: The 2022 regulations called the second KMP the "Compliance and Risk Manager". The 2025 text renamed it Compliance Officer. Old study material will betray you here.
cards.hook: PO owns everything; CO watches everything.

cards.title: The CO reports past the PO
cards.law: The Compliance Officer is a senior officer reporting to the board of directors — or the head of the organisation where there is no board.
cards.means: Independence is hard-wired: the person monitoring compliance does not report to the person running the funds. The CO must also be capable of understanding financial statements and the regulatory requirements.
cards.trip: 2022 said "financially literate and capable of appreciating"; 2025 sharpened it to "capable of understanding the financial statements". Small words, favourite trap.

cards.title: When two KMPs become three
cards.law: A Retail FME appoints an additional fund-management KMP BEFORE filing the offer document of its first retail scheme or ETF. Any FME crossing USD 1 billion AUM at FY-close (excluding FoF AUM) does the same.
cards.means: Scale and public money both demand a dedicated fund-management brain, separate from the PO.
cards.trip: The USD 1bn test EXCLUDES fund of funds AUM — those assets are managed at the underlying level. And the retail trigger is pre-FILING, not pre-launch.
cards.hook: Retail or a billion — either way, a third KMP.
cards.link: FoF look-through logic returns in valuation and custody (Module 9).

cards.title: Fit and proper — always, everyone

cards.title: Who gets in — and how many
cards.law: A VC scheme shall not have more than fifty (50) investors; non-accredited investors invest at least USD 250,000; FME employees/directors at USD 60,000.
cards.means: An exclusive room: 50 sophisticated cheques maximum. The 250K ticket is the sophistication filter; accredited investors skip it.
cards.trip: "At least" 250K — exactly 250K qualifies (2022 said "above"). And 2022 capped at 49 investors ("less than fifty"). Both flipped in 2025. Joint investors combining to 250K: only spouse, parent, or child.
cards.hook: 50 doors, 250K key, 60K staff entrance.

cards.title: The size of the pool
cards.law: Minimum corpus USD 3 Million; total corpus shall not exceed USD 200 Million.
cards.means: Both a floor and a ceiling — VC is the only mainstream scheme with a cap. Bigger ambitions route through restricted schemes.
cards.trip: Restricted schemes share the 3M floor but have NO ceiling. Don’t transplant the 200M cap.
cards.link: The 3M floor returns with new teeth in Module 4 — the 2026 unlisted gate.

cards.title: The 80/10 rule — keeping venture "venture"
cards.law: At least 80% of corpus goes to investee companies within 10 years of incorporation (or schemes meeting that test).
cards.means: Four-fifths of the money must reach genuinely young companies. This is what stops a VC label on a late-stage PE fund.
cards.trip: Ten years from INCORPORATION of the investee — not from its funding round, not from scheme launch.
cards.hook: 80% young blood, 20% free play.

cards.title: Skin in the game
cards.law: FME/associate invests ≥2.5% of targeted corpus (≤USD 30M schemes) or ≥USD 750,000 (>USD 30M), never exceeding 10%.
cards.means: The manager eats its own cooking. The floor aligns incentives; the 10% ceiling stops the FME dominating its own fund.
cards.trip: USD 750,000 is just 2.5% of 30M, frozen. And relocated schemes (moving to IFSC from abroad) are exempt entirely.
cards.hook: 750K = 2.5% of 30M, frozen.

cards.title: Conflicts and rhythm
cards.law: Associate investments need prior approval of 75% of investors by value. NAV at least annually, documented methodology; valuation by independents; leverage as disclosed in the PPM.
cards.means: Conflicted deals are democratised, not banned. And the compliance rhythm is annual — venture portfolios don’t need daily NAVs, they need methodological discipline.
cards.trip: 75% by VALUE, PRIOR — ratification after the cheque doesn’t cure it. And "VC schemes can’t borrow" is a myth: leverage is a disclosure matter.
cards.hook: 75%-by-value is the regulations’ answer to every conflict — remember it once, use it everywhere.
cards.link: The same 75% lever: restricted-scheme associate trades (Module 4) and winding-up votes (Module 11).

cards.title: The bigger tent
cards.law: Restricted schemes may have up to 1,000 investors. Schemes filed as Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended; Category III may be open- or close-ended.
cards.means: Twenty times the VC room, same sophistication filter (private placement to accredited/threshold investors). Structure follows strategy: locked capital for illiquid Cat I/II plays; open-ended only for Cat III.
cards.trip: The 50-investor cap is VC-only. Retail schemes have no cap at all. Keep the three numbers separate: 50 / 1,000 / unlimited.
cards.hook: 50 → 1,000 → ∞ as you climb the scheme ladder.

cards.title: Start small, prove yourself
cards.law: An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investing at USD 1 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months.
cards.means: A two-step launch ladder: start at 1M, prove you can reach 3M within a year of the taken-on-record communication.
cards.trip: Post the January 2026 Amendment, unlisted securities are OFF-LIMITS until the 3M is actually achieved — commencing at 1M does not open the unlisted door.
cards.hook: 1M to start, 3M to touch unlisted.

cards.title: The 25% unlisted cap
cards.law: Open-ended restricted schemes cap unlisted securities at 25% of corpus — with a look-through exception for FoFs whose underlying open-ended schemes each respect the cap.
cards.means: Redemption liquidity and illiquid paper don’t mix, so open-ended structures get a hard limit. Close-ended schemes face no such cap.
cards.trip: The post-2026 test is TWO-step: (1) corpus ≥ 3M? If no — zero unlisted. (2) If yes — stay within 25%. Checking only the cap is the pre-amendment reflex.

cards.title: Doubled skin for open doors
cards.law: Close-ended: ≥2.5% or ≥USD 750K (>30M). Open-ended: ≥5% or ≥USD 1.5M (>30M). Both capped at 10%.
cards.means: When investors can redeem, manager-investor misalignment bites harder — so open-ended floors are exactly double the close-ended ones.
cards.trip: Same 750K logic as VC, but the open-ended big-scheme floor is 1.5M. Four numbers, one pattern: close 2.5%/750K, open 5%/1.5M.
cards.hook: Open-ended = close-ended × 2.

cards.title: Conflicted trades and co-investments
cards.law: Buying/selling from associates, other schemes, or a 50%+ committed investor needs 75%-by-value approval — EXCLUDING the conflicted investor’s votes. Co-investment via segregated portfolios must never be on more favourable terms than the common portfolio; SPV leverage as disclosed.
cards.means: The supermajority returns, now with a twist: the mega-investor whose trade it is doesn’t get to vote on it. And co-investors may get access, never advantage.
cards.trip: "Not more favourable" — identical terms are fine, better terms are the breach.
cards.link: You met 75%-by-value in Module 3. Here it excludes the conflicted voter — the framework’s refinement for bigger rooms.

cards.title: Public money, prior review
cards.law: No retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed with IFSCA at least 21 working days before launch, with fees; Authority comments must be incorporated BEFORE launch.
cards.means: Private placements get a green channel; public money gets a runway. The regulator reads before the public buys.

cards.title: The 20/25 rule
cards.law: At least 20 investors; no single investor above 25% — achieved within 6 months of closure of the offer.
cards.means: Genuine pooling, not one whale wearing a retail costume. The 6-month cure window makes the rule practical: a 30% investor at closing is curable, not fatal.

cards.title: Form and fiduciaries

cards.title: The distressed-asset specialist
cards.law: A special situation fund invests in special situation assets and may act as a resolution applicant under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
cards.means: The bridge between IFSC capital and Indian insolvency resolution — an SSF can walk into a CIRP and bid for the company itself.

cards.title: Locked capital, long game
cards.law: SSFs are close-ended only, minimum tenure 3 years; extension up to 2 years with two-thirds by value; beyond that, only willing investors stay and dissenters get an exit.
cards.means: Distressed strategies and redemption liquidity are structurally incompatible. The extension ladder ends in pure consent: past year five, nobody is locked in against their will.
cards.trip: Beyond the 2-year extension it is NOT another vote — it’s express consent of the willing plus an exit for the rest.

cards.title: The extension asymmetry — 2026’s sharpest trap
cards.law: If an SSF misses its minimum corpus, it has a ONE-TIME option to extend the PPM by 6 months at 50% of the fresh-scheme fee.
cards.means: This is the pre-2026 rule — and for SSFs it still IS the rule. The January 2026 Amendment moved VC and restricted schemes to multiple extensions (25% first, 50% after, filed while the PPM is valid) but left Reg. 55(3) untouched.
cards.trip: One framework, two extension regimes. If a question doesn’t specify the scheme type, the extension answer is "it depends" — and that’s the point.
cards.hook: Everyone upgraded to multi-extension in 2026 — except the SSF.

cards.law: Only Registered FMEs (Retail) may launch ETFs — draft offer document 21 working days before launch, 12-month validity, and MANDATORY listing on a recognised stock exchange.

cards.law: Gold and Silver ETFs: at least 90% of AUM in the metal or bullion instruments (including BDRs); exposure to ETCDs with that metal underlying capped at 10%.

cards.title: Fund of funds — the look-through machine

cards.law: Private placement: at least USD 250,000 per investor or accredited investors, maximum 50 — final placement memorandum filed within 10 working days of allotment. Public offers run the full review cycle.
cards.means: REITs and InvITs mirror the scheme logic: a fast sophisticated lane with post-facto filing, and a slow public lane with pre-facto everything.

cards.title: The public lane, step by step
cards.law: Draft offer document ≥30 working days before the formal filing; public comments ≥14 days on four websites; due diligence certificate by the IM or investment banker; Authority observations within 30 working days of filing or 21 from a satisfactory reply — whichever is LATER.
cards.means: A public offer is a sequence of checkpoints, each with an owner and a clock. The "whichever is later" formula means sloppy query responses restart the regulator’s clock, never shorten it.
cards.trip: The comment window is 14 DAYS; the draft filing runway is 30 WORKING days. Mixing the units is the classic error.

cards.trip: Miss the 1-year window and there’s no confirmatory-letter shortcut — the entire draft-and-observation cycle restarts.

cards.title: Who must have a custodian
cards.law: Independent custodian mandatory for: retail schemes; open-ended restricted schemes; and any scheme with AUM above USD 70 Million. FoF exemption where underlying schemes have custodians.
cards.means: Three triggers — public money, redemption pressure, and sheer size. Miss all three and custody is your choice, not your obligation.
cards.trip: The USD 70M trigger catches CLOSE-ended restricted schemes too, once they grow. "We’re close-ended so no custodian" is only half a rule.
cards.hook: Retail, open-ended, or 70M+ — any one triggers custody.

cards.title: Where the custodian sits — and the 24-month runway
cards.law: The custodian must be IFSC-based, except where local laws of the issuing jurisdiction mandate local custody. The 2026 Amendment gives 24 months (from 30.01.2026) to make the IFSC appointment, with regulated India/foreign custodians permitted in the interim.
cards.means: Onshoring custody to GIFT City, with a realistic transition. The local-law carve-out follows mandatory foreign rules, with information arrangements for IFSCA.
cards.trip: The old Explanation II was substituted — if your compliance calendar still shows the pre-2026 transition, it’s wrong.

cards.title: Valuation: named independents, one schedule
cards.law: Assets valued per Sixth Schedule norms by an independent service provider: fund administrator, custodian, Authority-registered credit rating agency, or IBBI-registered valuer. FoF look-through exemption applies.
cards.means: Not "any independent person" — a closed list of four professional categories. Norms in the Sixth Schedule; execution by the named independents; obligation shared by FME and fiduciaries.
cards.trip: "Any SEBI-registered merchant banker" or "any CA" are not on the list — favourite wrong options.
cards.hook: Admin, custodian, CRA, IBBI valuer — the only four.

cards.title: The reporting clock

cards.title: The CEO cannot delegate the buck

cards.trip: Liability for acts in office SURVIVES termination and cannot be contracted away — no agreement, indemnity or resignation letter erases it. The FME also answers for its employees’ acts.

cards.law: Investors get holding statements at the end of every month, and within 10 working days on request. Fiduciaries must disclose anything with an adverse bearing on investments.

cards.title: Inspection — no trigger needed
cards.law: The Authority may appoint an Inspecting Authority suo motu, or on information or complaint, at ANY time — covering books, records, documents, infrastructure, procedures, systems, and associated entities. Everyone — PO, partners, trustees, directors, KMPs, employees, agents — must assist and give reasonable premises access.
cards.means: Inspection is not an event that requires cause; it’s a standing possibility. The cooperation duty reaches every human connected to the FME, down to agents.
cards.trip: "Only after a show-cause notice" is wrong; "only the compliance officer must cooperate" is wrong. No trigger, no narrow net.

cards.title: Winding up — three roads and a regulator’s hammer
cards.law: Grounds: tenure over; 75% of investors by value resolve; or (post-2026) funds raised but minimum corpus missed within the extended validity and the FME opts to wind up voluntarily. The Authority may also DIRECT winding up, merge schemes, or hand an FME’s schemes to ANOTHER FME to manage.
cards.means: Exit is as regulated as entry. The 2026 ground gives failed raises a clean statutory door. And the directive power to transplant scheme management is IFSC’s resolution mechanism for failing managers.
cards.trip: The investor vote is 75% by value — the same supermajority you’ve now seen in three modules. Retail extensions used 2/3; winding up uses 75%. Keep the fractions apart.
cards.link: That third ground exists BECAUSE of the multi-extension regime — Module 6’s asymmetry and Module 12’s tracker complete the picture.

cards.law: At its 29th meeting on 24 July 2026, the Authority approved a set of amendments to the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 aimed at ease of doing business, greater disclosure and regulatory clarity.
cards.means: Approval is the decision to amend. The binding text arrives only when the amendment is notified in the Gazette. Until then, the 2025 Regulations as amended to 30 January 2026 remain the operative law — every drill in Modules 1–12 still states the law that binds you today.

cards.title: The contribution ceiling moves 10% → 25%
cards.law: In place of the existing 10% limit, FMEs and their associates having Indian ultimate beneficial owners will be permitted to contribute up to 25% of the corpus of VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes, where such schemes invest only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions.
cards.means: Headroom for Indian-owned managers building an overseas track record. The floors (2.5% / 5% / USD 750K / USD 1.5M) are untouched — this raises the ceiling only, and only for a defined set.
cards.trip: It is conditional, not general: Indian UBO AND the scheme invests only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. cards.link: Modules 3 and 4 teach the binding 10% ceiling — that is still the examinable and enforceable figure.

cards.title: Timelines and valuation relax
cards.law: The scheme Annual Report timeline extends from four (4) to six (6) months from financial year end. Close-ended Restricted Schemes may move NAV computation and disclosure from semi-annual to annual, subject to prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. Independent valuation is relaxed for investments in underlying scheme(s) already valued by an independent entity.
cards.means: Three operational easements. Note the middle one is not automatic — it is unlocked by an investor supermajority, the framework's recurring 75%-by-value lever.
cards.trip: Until notified, Reg. 134's four-month clock governs. Diarise four months; plan for six.
cards.link: Module 9 drills the binding four-month clock.

cards.title: New structures: blended finance
cards.law: VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes will be permitted to issue multiple classes of units with differential distribution rights — junior / subordinate classes may carry returns lower than, or bear losses higher than, their entitlement. cards.hook: Junior units: USD 1Mn accredited (non-individual), USD 2Mn others.
